pitfalls.en: In Hebrew the perfect is not marked in the verb: the order of two past events is shown with words such as 'already' or 'before'. So an English sentence can lose its time order: *When I arrived, the train already left. English marks the earlier event with had + past participle: the train had already left.
pitfalls.he: בעברית אין סימון מיוחד בפועל ל'עבר שלפני העבר', והסדר מובע במילים כמו 'כבר' או 'קודם'. באנגלית מסמנים את האירוע המוקדם בפועל עצמו, עם had + V3: the train had already left.

pitfalls.en: In Hebrew one past form covers both 'I knew him' and 'I had known him'. In English, a period lasting up to a past moment needs the past perfect: I had known Amir for ten years when we started the company (not *I knew Amir for ten years when...).
pitfalls.he: בעברית צורת עבר אחת ('הכרתי אותו עשר שנים') משמשת לשני המקרים. באנגלית, תקופה שנמשכה עד רגע מסוים בעבר דורשת past perfect: I had known Amir for ten years.

pitfalls.en: In Hebrew the perfect is not marked in the verb, and the same conditional structure can describe the present or the past. In English the past needs had + past participle and would have: If I had known, I would have come (not *If I knew, I would come, when you mean yesterday).
pitfalls.he: בעברית אין סימון של 'עבר שלפני העבר' בפועל, ואותו מבנה ('לו ידעתי, הייתי בא') מתאים גם להווה וגם לעבר. באנגלית, תנאי על העבר דורש had + V3 ו-would have: If I had known.

pitfalls.en: In Hebrew the progressive and perfect are not marked in the verb. One present passive form covers 'houses are built' (in general) and 'a house is being built' (now), and one past form covers 'was built' and 'has been built'. English must choose: The stadium is being built at the moment (not *The stadium is built at the moment).
pitfalls.he: בעברית אין סימון של הווה מתמשך או של perfect בפועל: 'נבנה' יכול לתאר מצב כללי, פעולה שקורית עכשיו או פעולה שהסתיימה. באנגלית חייבים לבחור, ולמה שקורה עכשיו אומרים is being built.

pitfalls.en: Hebrew reported speech keeps the speaker's original tense (word for word: 'Last summer Kenji asked me where I am staying'). In English, after a past reporting verb the tense usually shifts back: Last summer, Kenji asked me where I was staying.
pitfalls.he: בדיבור עקיף בעברית הזמן המקורי נשמר ('בקיץ שעבר קנג׳י שאל אותי איפה אני מתאכסן'). באנגלית, אחרי פועל דיווח בעבר, הזמן בדרך כלל זז אחורה: where I was staying.

pitfalls.en: In Hebrew questions the verb often comes before a noun subject ('when opens the museum?'), and learners carry this into reported questions: *She asked when opened the museum. In English the subject always comes before the verb: She asked when the museum opened.
pitfalls.he: בשאלות בעברית הפועל בא לעתים קרובות לפני נושא שהוא שם עצם ('מתי נפתח המוזיאון?'). באנגלית הנושא תמיד בא לפני הפועל: She asked when the museum opened.

pitfalls.en: Hebrew often links the two halves of a sentence with a pair of words (literally 'admittedly ..., but ...'), so learners write *Although the course was expensive, but it was worth it. English uses one connector only: Although the course was expensive, it was worth it. / The course was expensive, but it was worth it.
pitfalls.he: בעברית מקובל לחבר את שני חלקי המשפט בשתי מילות קישור ('אמנם הקורס יקר, אבל...'). באנגלית משתמשים במילת קישור אחת בלבד: although או but, לא שתיהן.

pitfalls.en: In Hebrew there is no indefinite article, so 'a' can drop out of fixed phrases: *make decision, *take break, *have look. When the noun is singular and countable, English collocations keep a/an: make a decision, take a break, have a look.
pitfalls.he: בעברית אין מילה ל-a, ולכן קל להשמיט אותה גם בצירופים קבועים. באנגלית, כששם העצם ביחיד וספיר, ה-a נשארת: make a decision, take a break.

pitfalls.en: Hebrew has one verb, 'do', where English has two, make and do, so learners often say *do a mistake or *do an effort. English uses make for these: make a mistake, make an effort, make progress. Do is for tasks and work: do homework, do research.
pitfalls.he: בעברית יש פועל אחד, 'לעשות', ובאנגלית יש שניים: make ו-do. טעויות ומאמץ 'עושים' עם make (make a mistake), ואת do שומרים למשימות ולעבודה (do homework).

pitfalls.en: Hebrew uses 'strong' with rain, cold and pain, so learners write *strong rain or *strong cold. English chooses a different adjective for each noun: heavy rain, bitter (or freezing) cold, severe pain.
pitfalls.he: בעברית אומרים גשם חזק, קור חזק וכאב חזק, אבל באנגלית strong לא מתאים לכולם: לכל שם עצם יש שם תואר משלו, כמו heavy rain ו-severe pain.

pitfalls.en: Many Hebrew idioms mean nothing in English when they are translated word for word: *It was on the face (for 'it was terrible') or *It's coming out of my nose (for 'I'm sick of it'). Translate the meaning, not the words: It was terrible. I'm sick of it.
pitfalls.he: ניבים עבריים רבים, כמו 'על הפנים' או 'יצא לי מהאף', לא אומרים כלום באנגלית בתרגום מילה במילה. תרגמו את המשמעות ולא את המילים: It was terrible.

pitfalls.en: In Hebrew there are no capital letters, and informal English messages often drop them too (hi dana, i'll be late). In a formal email, capitals are required: Dear Ms Cohen, the pronoun I, names, days and months (Monday, March) and the first word of the sign-off (Kind regards).
pitfalls.he: בעברית אין אותיות גדולות, וגם בהודעות לא רשמיות באנגלית משמיטים אותן לעיתים קרובות. במייל רשמי הן חובה: בפנייה (Dear Ms Cohen), בכינוי I, בשמות, בימים ובחודשים ובמילה הראשונה בסיום.

pitfalls.en: In Hebrew, an imperative softened with bevakasha ('please') is polite enough in many situations. Translated word for word, 'Please send me the slides' can sound like an order to someone you don't know or who is doing you a favour. In English, ask a question or hedge: Could you send me the slides? / I was wondering if you could send me the slides.
pitfalls.he: בעברית 'תשלח לי בבקשה את המצגת' היא בקשה מנומסת מספיק במצבים רבים. בתרגום מילולי, ציווי עם please עלול להישמע כמו הוראה כשפונים למישהו שאינכם מכירים או למי שעושה לכם טובה. באנגלית שואלים שאלה או מרככים: Could you send me the slides?

pitfalls.en: In Hebrew, ani rotse / ani rotsa ('I want') is a normal, polite way to make a request, even to a company. In an English request, 'I want' sounds demanding. Use I would like or a hedged question: I would like to request a refund, not I want a refund.
pitfalls.he: בעברית 'אני רוצה' היא דרך ניטרלית לבקש משהו, אבל בפנייה באנגלית I want נשמע תובעני. השתמשו ב-I would like או בשאלה מרוככת.

pitfalls.en: The Hebrew reporting verb to'en / to'enet is everyday and often neutral (the researcher to'enet that ... = the researcher argues that ...), so learners tend to translate it as claim every time. In English, claims suggests that the writer doubts the statement. For neutral reporting use says, states or argues, and keep claims for when you really mean to signal doubt.
pitfalls.he: בעברית 'טוען' הוא פועל דיווח שכיח, ולעיתים קרובות ניטרלי ('החוקרת טוענת ש...'), ולכן קל לתרגם אותו תמיד ל-claims. באנגלית claims מרמז שהכותב מפקפק בטענה. לדיווח ניטרלי השתמשו ב-says, states או argues, ושמרו את claims למקרים שבהם אתם באמת רוצים להביע ספק.

prompt.en: Read the sentence. Which event happened first?

ex.question: When Dana arrived at the party, her friends had gone home.
options: Her friends went home.
Dana arrived at the party.
Both happened at exactly the same time.

1.en: Dana arriving is the story's 'now' (past simple). Had gone takes us back to an earlier time: her friends left first.

2.en: For two things happening together we would use the past continuous: When Dana arrived, her friends were leaving. Had gone means they had left before she arrived.

explanation.en: had + past participle (had gone) = earlier than the other past event (arrived). By the time Dana got there, her friends were no longer at the party.

options: She overslept and missed her bus.
Her taxi got stuck in marathon traffic.
The buses weren't running, and finding a taxi took time.
She waited at the wrong bus stop.

0.en: She doesn't mention sleeping late. She had been waiting at the bus stop for twenty minutes.

1.en: The marathon stopped the buses. She doesn't say the taxi was slow: by the time she found one, the meeting had started.

3.en: She was at a normal stop; the problem was that the buses weren't running at all.

explanation.en: I'd been waiting ... when someone told me = an activity in progress up to a past moment. By the time I found a taxi, you'd already started = the meeting started before she found a taxi. In both, I'd and you'd = had.

prompt.en: Choose the best option.

2.en: Has written connects to now. Her twentieth birthday is a past moment, so step back from it: had written.

explanation.en: by the time + past simple (turned) → past perfect in the main clause for what was already complete at that moment.

prompt.en: Read the sentence. What do we know about Maya?

ex.question: If Maya had taken the job, she would be living in London now.
options: She took the job and lives in London.
She didn't take the job, and she doesn't live in London.
She may take the job and move to London.
She didn't take the job, but she lives in London anyway.

0.en: Conditionals with had + past participle are unreal: the opposite happened. She did not take the job.

2.en: That would be a first conditional about the future (If Maya takes the job, she will...). Had taken refers to the past.

3.en: The main clause (would be living in London now) is unreal too: she isn't living there.

explanation.en: Mixed conditional: an unreal past condition (had taken) with an unreal present result (would be living ... now). In reality: no job, no London.

prompt.en: Sort the connectors by the relationship they show.

explanation.en: Contrast compares two different things (whereas, in contrast). Concession admits a point and gives an unexpected result (nevertheless, even though). Owing to and because of give the reason; consequently and as a result give the effect.

prompt.en: Choose the connector that fits the logic and the grammar.

ex.question: Maya's flat is right in the city centre, ___ Lior's is a forty-minute bus ride away.
options: nevertheless
whereas
furthermore
consequently

0.en: Nevertheless shows an unexpected result, and as a sentence connector it cannot join two clauses after a comma. Here we are simply comparing two flats.

2.en: Furthermore adds a point in the same direction, and it cannot join two clauses after a comma. These two facts are different, not added together.

3.en: Consequently shows a result, but where Maya lives does not cause where Lior lives. It also cannot join two clauses after a comma.

explanation.en: Whereas compares two different things inside one sentence: A is X, whereas B is Y. It is a conjunction, so a comma before it is correct.

options: In contrast,
Consequently,
Furthermore,

1.en: Consequently means 'because of this'. Free entry would not cause fewer visitors; the logic points the other way.

2.en: Furthermore adds a point that supports the first one. Few visitors is not an extra advantage; it is unexpected.

hint.en: Free entry should attract visitors. Is the second fact expected or surprising?

explanation.en: Free entry should bring visitors, but it does not: that is concession. Nevertheless (or However, Even so) introduces the unexpected result.

tokens: Many teenagers now get their news from short videos on social media.
This habit has obvious advantages: the videos are quick, free and easy to share.

As a result, viewers may find it hard to tell a reliable report from a rumour.
Schools could therefore teach students to check a story before sharing it.

explanation.en: The first sentence introduces the topic. 'This habit' points back to it; 'However, such clips' turns to the problem; 'As a result' gives its effect; 'therefore' introduces the conclusion.

options: Online courses are flexible, cheap and available almost anywhere. Their main weakness is isolation: many learners miss the face-to-face contact of a classroom. Nevertheless, for people with jobs or families, this flexibility often matters more.

2.en: Consequently is illogical (being cheap does not make courses available everywhere), and 'Whereas many learners miss ...' is not a complete sentence.

3.en: Moreover, however and nevertheless cannot join clauses with commas, so this is one long run-on sentence.

explanation.en: The best version lists the advantages in one sentence, uses 'this flexibility' to point back, and needs only one connector (Nevertheless) at the point where the argument turns.

prompt.en: You are texting a close friend. Which message sounds natural?

options: I regret to inform you that I will be unable to attend this evening's dinner.

I am writing to inform you that I cannot come to dinner tonight.

0.en: Perfect in a formal email, but to a close friend 'I regret to inform you' sounds cold, as if you were cancelling a business contract.

3.en: 'I am writing to inform you' is a formal email opening; nobody 'writes to inform' a friend by text.

explanation.en: Friends expect informal language: a contraction (can't), a set phrase (make it = manage to come), short sentences and an exclamation mark. Too much formality is a register mistake too: it creates distance.

0.en: This is an opinion, but it is honestly marked as one: In my view.

1.en: This is a factual claim: you can check the date.

3.en: This reports what some drivers say. Whether the rules are confusing is their opinion, but the fact that they say so can be checked.

explanation.en: 'Everyone knows' presents a judgement (pointless) as something nobody could disagree with. A careful writer would say who thinks so, or mark it clearly as an opinion.

prompt.en: Same thing, different spin. Is each phrase positive, neutral or negative?

explanation.en: Each group describes the same thing. Bold, cosy and lively invite you to approve; reckless, cramped and shouting match invite you to disapprove; the neutral words leave the judgement to you. An estate agent says cosy; an unhappy tenant says cramped.

prompt.en: Match each loaded word with a neutral word that a careful reporter might use.

explanation.en: The loaded words add feeling: slash (violent), mob (dangerous and out of control), scrap (worthless), flood (overwhelming), rant (angry and unreasonable), hike (sudden and unfair). The neutral words describe the same facts and let readers decide.

prompt.en: Listen to part of a radio report and answer the question.

ex.audio_text: The company claims its new app helps users sleep better. In a survey it carried out itself, most users said they felt more rested. However, independent researchers point out that the survey did not include anyone who wasn't using the app.
ex.question: What does the reporter suggest about the company's evidence?
options: It proves that the app works.
It may be weak, because the company ran its own survey and did not compare users with non-users.
It comes from independent researchers.
It shows that most users slept worse.

0.en: The reporter uses 'claims' and then gives the researchers' objection, so the evidence is presented as doubtful, not as proof.

2.en: The company carried out the survey itself; the independent researchers only criticise it.

3.en: The users said they felt more rested, not worse.

hint.en: Listen for the reporting verbs: claims, point out.

explanation.en: Three clues: 'claims' signals doubt; 'carried out itself' shows that the source has an interest in the result; and 'point out' tells you the reporter accepts the researchers' criticism. Without a comparison group, you cannot tell whether the app made any difference.

prompt.en: Read for the writer's stance.

ex.question: A journalist writes: 'The minister admitted that the project was over budget.' What does 'admitted' tell you?
options: The minister was proud of the project's cost.
The journalist thinks the minister is lying.
The minister refused to answer the question.
The fact is embarrassing for the minister, and the journalist treats it as true.

0.en: Admit is used for something negative or embarrassing, not something you are proud of.

1.en: If the journalist doubted it, a verb like 'claimed' would be more likely. 'Admitted' presents the statement as true.

2.en: Admitted means the minister did say it, even if unwillingly.

explanation.en: Admit = say, often unwillingly, that something bad is true. Compare: the minister said (neutral), claimed (the writer has doubts), revealed (new and true), admitted (negative and true).

prompt.en: Spot the selective evidence.

ex.question: An advert says: 'Sales of our bike helmet rose by 200% last year!' What important information is missing?
options: How many helmets were sold before the rise
The colour of the helmet
The price of the helmet
Where the helmets are sold

1.en: The colour doesn't affect whether the number is impressive.

2.en: The price might matter to a buyer, but it doesn't tell you whether 200% is a big rise.

3.en: Where they are sold doesn't tell you whether 200% is a big change.

explanation.en: A percentage without the starting number can mislead: a 200% rise could be from 1,000 to 3,000 helmets, or from 5 to 15. Always ask: 200% of what?

prompt.en: Think about the source and its purpose.

ex.question: You want a balanced view of a new electric scooter. Which source is most likely to be one-sided?
options: A comparison of five scooters by an independent consumer magazine
A news report on the scooter's launch that quotes both fans and critics
A press release from the company that makes the scooter
A forum where owners post both good and bad reviews

0.en: An independent comparison has no reason to favour one product, so it is a good place to start.

1.en: A report that quotes both sides is trying to be balanced.

3.en: Individual reviews can be biased, but a mix of good and bad reviews gives you several viewpoints.

explanation.en: A press release is written by the organisation itself to show its product in the best light. It may be accurate, but you should look for the other side elsewhere.

prompt.en: Rewrite the loaded news sentence in neutral language. Choose words from the box. Three words are not needed.

ex.text: Loaded: 'The council has slashed the youth budget and scrapped the free night bus, while a mob of furious parents gathered outside.' Neutral: 'The council has ___ the youth budget and ___ the free night bus, while a ___ of parents gathered outside.'
answers: reduced
cut
cancelled
canceled
ended
withdrawn
discontinued
crowd
group

wrong_feedback.match: axed

feedback.en: Axed is as loaded as scrapped: it suggests something was chopped off violently. Neutral: cancelled.

wrong_feedback.match: gutted

feedback.en: Gutted is loaded: it suggests the budget was destroyed from the inside. Neutral: reduced.

wrong_feedback.match: horde

feedback.en: Horde is loaded: it suggests a large, threatening group. Neutral: crowd.

explanation.en: slashed → reduced, scrapped → cancelled, mob → crowd. Notice that 'furious' has gone too: a neutral report describes what happened and leaves the feelings to the reader, or to a quote from the parents.

prompt.en: This sentence presents an opinion as a fact. Rewrite it as a clearly marked opinion: start with 'In my view,' or 'In my opinion,' and remove the word that makes it sound like a fact. Change nothing else.

ex.source: Obviously, the new stadium is a waste of money.
answers: In my view, the new stadium is a waste of money.
In my view the new stadium is a waste of money.
In my opinion, the new stadium is a waste of money.
In my opinion the new stadium is a waste of money.

wrong_feedback.match: In my view, the new stadium is waste of money.

feedback.en: Keep the article: a waste of money.

wrong_feedback.match: obviously

feedback.en: Remove obviously: it tells readers that no sensible person could disagree, which is exactly what makes an opinion sound like a fact.

hint.en: Which word tells the reader that nobody could disagree?

explanation.en: 'Obviously' hides the fact that this is a judgement. 'In my view' is honest about it and invites the reader to weigh your reasons. In an essay, you would then give those reasons.

prompt.en: This sentence is from a news report, not an opinion column. Remove the reporter's opinion.

ex.sentence: The mayor's ridiculous new parking plan will come into force in May.
answers: The mayor's new parking plan will come into force in May.

hint.en: One word is the reporter's judgement, not a fact.

explanation.en: 'Ridiculous' is an opinion. A news report should state what will happen and let people who dislike the plan say so in a quote: 'Some residents called the plan ridiculous.'

prompt.en: Which of these could work as the thesis of an argumentative essay? Sort them.

items.text: Schools should drop compulsory uniforms, because they cost families money and do little to improve behaviour.
Public transport should be free for students under 25, because it would cut traffic and widen access to education.
Our city opened a light rail line last year.
In this essay, I will discuss school uniforms.
Homework has both advantages and disadvantages.
This essay is about the four-day working week.
Social media is an interesting topic with many sides.

explanation.en: A strong thesis takes a position that a reasonable person could disagree with, and gives reasons. A fact cannot be argued; an announcement only names the topic; 'advantages and disadvantages' sits on the fence.

prompt.en: Choose the strongest thesis.

ex.question: Essay question: 'Should final exams be replaced by coursework?'
options: Exams and coursework are two different ways of assessing students.
Coursework is good, and exams are bad.
Final exams should be partly replaced by coursework, because coursework measures skills such as research and planning that a three-hour exam cannot.
Everyone agrees that exams are stressful, so they should be abolished.

0.en: This is a fact, not a position. Nobody could disagree with it, so there is nothing to argue.

1.en: This takes a side, but it is vague (good in what way?) and gives no reason.

3.en: It gives a reason, but 'everyone agrees' is not evidence, and stress alone doesn't show that exams should disappear completely.

explanation.en: The strongest thesis is specific (partly replaced), debatable and gives a reason that the body paragraphs can develop.

prompt.en: Claim: 'The school canteen should offer a cheaper vegetarian dish every day.' Does each piece of support help this claim?

items.text: In a survey by the student council, many students said they skip lunch because the meals are too expensive.
The canteen manager says a daily vegetarian dish could be offered at a lower price than the meat dishes.
Students who skip lunch because of the price often find it harder to concentrate in afternoon lessons.
My cousin became a vegetarian last year.
The canteen was painted green last summer.
A famous footballer said on TV that vegetables are the future.

hint.en: Ask two questions: does it support this exact claim (a cheaper vegetarian dish), and would it convince someone who disagrees?

explanation.en: Relevant support connects directly to the claim: students want cheaper food, the dish is affordable, and eating lunch matters. A single personal story, what 'everyone I know' likes, an unrelated fact and a celebrity who is not an expert on school meals do not prove anything about this claim.

prompt.en: Put the sentences in order to make a PEEL paragraph: Point, Evidence, Explain, Link.

tokens: The main advantage of coursework is that it rewards skills that matter after school.
For example, in her history project Maya had to plan her time over six weeks, find and evaluate her own sources and rewrite her first draft after feedback.
None of these skills can be tested in a three-hour exam, yet universities and employers expect all of them.
For this reason, coursework should count for at least part of the final grade.

hint.en: Look for the words that point back or forward: For example, these skills, For this reason.

explanation.en: Point (the main advantage of coursework) → Evidence (For example, Maya's project) → Explain (none of these skills can be tested in an exam, but they are needed later) → Link (For this reason, coursework should count). 'These skills' points back to the example, and 'For this reason' introduces the link to the thesis.

prompt.en: Listen to a student answering an objection in a debate.

ex.audio_text: I accept that a four-day school week would be difficult for some working parents. That's a real concern. But schools could run clubs and sports on the fifth day, and in my view, the benefit of rested, motivated students is far greater than the cost of organising them.
ex.question: How does the speaker answer the objection?
options: By showing that the objection is factually wrong
By ignoring it and changing the subject
By changing position and now opposing the plan
By accepting it and arguing that the benefits are greater

0.en: The speaker says 'I accept that ...' and calls it 'a real concern', so the objection is not rejected as wrong.

1.en: The speaker answers the objection directly, with a practical solution and a comparison.

2.en: The speaker still supports the four-day week.

explanation.en: This is concede and outweigh: 'I accept that ... That's a real concern' (concede), then 'the benefit ... is far greater than the cost' (outweigh). The practical suggestion (clubs on the fifth day) makes the rebuttal stronger, because it reduces the problem as well as weighing it.

prompt.en: How does each response answer the objection in quotation marks? Sort them by rebuttal move.

items.text: 'Coursework is easy to copy.' However, this overlooks the fact that teachers see drafts at every stage, which makes copying hard to hide.
'A phone ban makes emergencies impossible to handle.' In fact, students can still use the school office phone, and parents can call the office.
'Free transport would cost the city money.' That is true; nevertheless, cleaner air and quieter streets are worth more than the cost.
'A later start is inconvenient for some parents.' Admittedly, it is. Even so, the benefits for students' learning outweigh this inconvenience.
'Young children cannot travel to school alone.' This is a fair concern, so the later start should apply only to students aged 15 and over.
'Some students need their phones for medical apps.' Critics are right about this, so the ban should include exceptions for health reasons.

explanation.en: Refute: the objection is wrong (However, this overlooks ... / In fact ...). Concede and outweigh: it is true, but something else matters more (nevertheless, even so, outweigh). Qualify: it is partly true, so the claim becomes narrower (should apply only to ... / should include exceptions).

prompt.en: Which sentence states the counterargument fairly?

ex.question: Your thesis: 'Schools should ban phones during lessons.' Which sentence presents the opposing view best?
options: Some people think teenagers should be allowed to stare at screens all day.
Critics argue that a ban removes a useful learning tool and takes away students' chance to learn self-control.
Opponents of the ban are probably just addicted to their own phones.
Obviously, nobody seriously believes that phones help learning.

0.en: This is a straw man: nobody argues for screens all day. A caricature is easy to defeat, but it convinces no one.

2.en: This attacks the people, not their argument.

3.en: This dismisses the other side instead of stating it. Many teachers do use phones in lessons, so readers will notice the gap.

explanation.en: A fair counterargument is attributed (Critics argue) and gives the strongest version of the other side, as its supporters would put it. Answering a strong objection makes your own argument more convincing.

prompt.en: Choose the strongest rebuttal.

ex.question: Counterargument: 'Critics argue that making public transport free for under-25s would cost the city too much.'
options: It is true that the scheme would cost money; however, if more young people left their cars at home, the city would spend less on road repairs and parking, which would cover part of the cost.
This argument is wrong, and critics should think about the planet instead.
Many cities around the world have free transport, so it must be a good idea.
Money is not important when young people's futures are at stake.

1.en: This dismisses the objection and gives no reason. Telling critics what to think about is not a rebuttal.

2.en: Popularity is not evidence: what works in one city may not work in another, and the cost question is still unanswered.

3.en: Cost does matter to a city, so brushing it aside makes the argument look weak. This avoids the objection instead of answering it.

explanation.en: The strongest rebuttal concedes the point fairly ('It is true that the scheme would cost money') and then answers it with reasoning: savings on roads and parking would reduce the real cost. It responds to the objection instead of avoiding it.

prompt.en: Choose the strongest conclusion.

ex.question: Thesis: 'Public transport should be free for everyone under 25, because it would cut traffic and make education and jobs easier to reach.' Which conclusion works best?
options: In conclusion, public transport should be free for everyone under 25, because it would cut traffic and make education and jobs easier to reach.
In conclusion, free public transport would cut traffic. Another advantage is that tourists would find it much easier to get around the city.

In conclusion, free transport for under-25s would ease congestion and put colleges and workplaces within reach of young people who cannot afford to travel. A city that wants its young people to study and work should make it easy for them to get there.
In conclusion, there are strong arguments on both sides of this debate, so it is difficult to say whether free transport is a good idea.

0.en: This copies the thesis word for word. Restate it in new words, then end with a final thought about why it matters.

1.en: Tourists are a new argument, and one that has nothing to do with under-25s. A conclusion sums up; it does not start a point that it has no room to support.

3.en: After arguing for free transport, the writer suddenly sits on the fence. The conclusion should confirm the thesis, not abandon it.

explanation.en: The strongest conclusion restates the thesis in new words (ease congestion, within reach of young people), sums up both reasons and ends with a final implication. It adds no new argument and does not reopen the debate.

prompt.en: Complete the counterargument and rebuttal with words from the box. Three words are not needed.

ex.text: ___ argue that coursework is unfair to students who get little help at home. This is a fair point; ___, the same is true of exams, since private tutoring improves exam results as well. ___, coursework could be done in school, under supervision, which would reduce the advantage of outside help.
answers: Critics
Opponents
Some people
Some
however
nevertheless
even so
Moreover
Furthermore
In addition
What is more
Besides

wrong_feedback.match: Everyone

feedback.en: 'Everyone argue' is ungrammatical (everyone argues), and it overstates the case. Attribute the view to a specific group, such as critics.

wrong_feedback.match: therefore

feedback.en: Therefore introduces a result, but these sentences answer or add to the objection; they don't follow from it. Use however for the contrast and Moreover to add a point.

wrong_feedback.match: Obviously

feedback.en: Obviously dismisses instead of arguing, and it doesn't add a new point. You need an addition connector: Moreover.

wrong_feedback.match: Moreover

feedback.en: Moreover adds a point on the same side. After conceding ('This is a fair point'), you need a contrast to turn to your answer: however. Moreover belongs in gap 3, where you add a second answer.

wrong_feedback.match: however

feedback.en: However signals a contrast, so it belongs in gap 2, where you turn from the concession to your answer. Gap 3 adds a second answer, so it needs Moreover.

hint.en: Gap 1 attributes the opposing view, gap 2 turns to your answer, gap 3 adds a second answer.

explanation.en: Critics argue (attribute the opposing view) → This is a fair point; however, ... (concede, then answer) → Moreover, ... (add a second answer). Note the punctuation: a semicolon before however, and a comma after however and Moreover.

prompt.en: Combine the two ideas into one concede-and-outweigh sentence. Start with 'It is true that' and join the ideas with '; nevertheless,'.

ex.source: (1) A later start would be inconvenient for some parents. (2) The benefits for students' learning are greater.
answers: It is true that a later start would be inconvenient for some parents; nevertheless, the benefits for students' learning are greater.
It is true that a later start would be inconvenient for some parents; nevertheless the benefits for students' learning are greater.
It is true that a later start would be inconvenient for some parents. Nevertheless, the benefits for students' learning are greater.

wrong_feedback.match: It is true that a later start would be inconvenient for some parents, nevertheless, the benefits for students' learning are greater.

feedback.en: A comma cannot join two complete sentences, even with nevertheless. Use a semicolon (; nevertheless,) or a full stop.

wrong_feedback.match: It is true that a later start would be inconvenient for some parents, but nevertheless the benefits for students' learning are greater.

feedback.en: Use one connector, not two. The task pattern is: ... parents; nevertheless, the benefits ...

wrong_feedback.match: Although a later start would be inconvenient for some parents, the benefits for students' learning are greater.

feedback.en: That is a correct concession sentence, but this task practises a different pattern: It is true that ...; nevertheless, ...

hint.en: Pattern: It is true that + idea 1; nevertheless, + idea 2.

explanation.en: 'It is true that' concedes the objection; '; nevertheless,' turns to your answer and shows that it outweighs the objection. Keep the semicolon before nevertheless and the comma after it.

prompt.en: Correct the mistake in this sentence from an essay.

ex.sentence: There are many evidences that the new timetable has improved attendance.
answers: There is a lot of evidence that the new timetable has improved attendance.
There is much evidence that the new timetable has improved attendance.
There is plenty of evidence that the new timetable has improved attendance.
There is considerable evidence that the new timetable has improved attendance.
There is strong evidence that the new timetable has improved attendance.
There is substantial evidence that the new timetable has improved attendance.
There is a great deal of evidence that the new timetable has improved attendance.
There is evidence that the new timetable has improved attendance.
There are many pieces of evidence that the new timetable has improved attendance.

wrong_feedback.match: evidences

feedback.en: Evidence has no plural form. Use There is + evidence: There is considerable evidence that ...

wrong_feedback.match: many

feedback.en: Many goes with plural countable nouns, but evidence is uncountable. Use much, a lot of, considerable or strong: There is considerable evidence that ... (or many pieces of evidence).

hint.en: Can you count evidence? Check the noun and the verb.

explanation.en: Evidence is uncountable: no plural -s, and a singular verb. There is considerable (or strong, or a lot of) evidence that ... For one item, say a piece of evidence. In a formal essay, considerable or strong sounds better than a lot of.
